summary: Describes a protocol for adding integrity assurance to files distributed across the Internet, so users can check that what they got was unaltered, no matter which mirror it came from. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A tamper-proof seal on a package that stays the same no matter which shop gave it to you.

questions: how to verify the integrity of downloaded files
how do i verify a downloaded file has not been modified
how does the betsi system work
subtitle: A protocol for proving files have not been tampered with, no matter where they come from.

tldr.problem: Software and data distributed over the Internet can be modified maliciously. A user has no way to know whether a file they download has been changed in transit or on a mirror server.
tldr.mechanism: An author submits a cryptographic hash of their file to a trusted third party, which signs and seals it. The author then distributes the file with the sealed certificate. Users verify the certificate against the third party's public key and check the hash of the file they received.
tldr.outcome: A user can prove a file has not been tampered with, even when downloaded from an untrusted location or mirror, as long as they trust the third party's verification process.

today: RFC 1805 is an Informational document describing a protocol framework. It has not been obsoleted. While the Betsi implementation remains available, modern practice typically uses digital signatures and certificates (such as X.509) with certificate authorities rather than this specific protocol.

sections.title: The Challenge of Verifying File Integrity
sections.content:
The RFC identifies a fundamental security problem: when a user downloads software, data or any file from the Internet, they want to know whether the file has been corrupted accidentally or modified maliciously. The obvious answer—run verification software—fails because the verification software itself could have been compromised. This creates a chicken-and-egg problem: you cannot trust the tool that verifies integrity if that tool might also have been attacked.

The protocol described in RFC 1805 solves this by using a trusted third party and by encoding integrity proofs in ASCII messages that can be verified independently without special software, using only widely available standards. The RFC notes an existing implementation called Betsi, operational since August 1994.
sections.eli5: You might download a program and run it to check if a file is safe. But what if someone changed that program? This RFC shows a different way: have an official seal the file before it goes out.

sections.title: How the Protocol Works
sections.content:
The protocol involves three parties: an Author who distributes files, a User who wants to verify integrity, and a Trusted third party (T) who certifies files. The protocol consists of five phases, though only four are fully specified; the second phase (author verification) is intentionally left open for different implementations.

An author first registers with the trusted party and provides their name, organization, contact information, and a public signature key. The trusted party verifies the author's identity using whatever method is appropriate (in Betsi, verification is done by phone using the telephone company directory). Once verified, an author can submit file certificates at any time.
sections.eli5: First, authors register their name and who they are. The trusted party checks they are real people. Then authors can get their files sealed.

sections.title: File Certification and Distribution
sections.content:
To certify a file, an author computes a cryptographic hash (using MD5, SHA, or another algorithm) of the file contents and signs a message containing the author's name, the hash function used, the file location, and one or more entries giving the hash, file name, and optional version number for each file. The author sends this signed message to the trusted third party.

The trusted party verifies the author's signature, then creates a location-independent certificate containing the trusted party's identity, the author's name, the author's organization, the hash function, the current date, and the list of hashes. The trusted party signs this certificate and returns it to the author. The author distributes the file with the sealed certificate alongside it. Because all information is in ASCII, it can be sent via email, FTP, HTTP, or any other means.
sections.eli5: The author does math on the file to make a fingerprint, signs it, and sends it to the trusted party. The trusted party adds the date and their official stamp, then sends it back.

sections.title: How Users Verify Files
sections.content:
A user who receives a file and a certificate follows these steps. First, they obtain the trusted party's public key from several independent sources to verify its authenticity. Second, they use that key to verify the signature on the certificate and examine whether they trust the method the trusted party used to verify the author's identity (recorded in the certificate). Third, they extract the hash function and hash values from the certificate, then compute the same hash function on the file they received. If the hashes match, the file has not been modified.

As a final safeguard, the user checks the trusted party's certificate revocation list (CRL) to confirm that the certificate has not been revoked due to a compromised key or an author losing legitimacy. If all checks pass and no assumptions have been violated, the user is assured of both the integrity and the time at which the file was certified.
sections.eli5: You get the official's public key from a few places to make sure it is real. You check the signature on the seal. You do the same fingerprint math on the file you got and see if it matches. If yes, the file is safe.

sections.title: Author Verification Methods
sections.content:
Phase II (author verification) is intentionally not fully specified in the RFC. Different implementations may verify author identity using different methods. The Betsi implementation uses the public telephone infrastructure: the trusted party calls directory assistance to obtain the author's phone number, calls the author, and asks them to confirm information sent in their registration. The author may provide their own public key or have the trusted party assign one.

The RFC acknowledges that Betsi only operates in the United States and notes that international verification standards need to be developed. Whatever method is used is recorded in each certificate, so users know what verification procedure was followed. This makes the protocol flexible: the certification and verification logic works with any signature scheme and any author verification method, as long as both are recorded in the certificate.
sections.eli5: The trusted party needs to make sure you really are who you say you are. Betsi calls you on the phone to check. Other methods could work too, as long as they write down how they checked.
